e-151.problem:
A function $f(x)$ has values according to the table below:

| $x$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-1.0$ | $-0.7$ | $-0.3$ | $0.7$ | $1.5$ | $2.1$ |

Approximate  at the point $x=3$ using a forward difference approximation.
e-151.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation formula

$$
f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}
$$

 

at the point $x=3.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & ≈\frac{f(3+1)-f(3)}{1} \\  & =\frac{f(4)-f(3)}{1} \\  & =\frac{(-0.3)-(-0.7)}{1} \\  & =\frac{0.4}{1} \\  & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

e-153.knowledge_point: Estimating a Derivative From a Table Using a Forward Difference Approximation: Word Problem
e-153.problem:
The position of a race car along a straight track, measured in feet from the starting line, is given by the function $s(t),$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. The values of $s(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below:

| $t$ | $0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $s(t)$ | $0$ | $3$ | $7$ | $12$ | $19$ |

Approximate the velocity $s'(t)$ at the time $t=0.1$ using a forward difference approximation.
e-153.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
s'(t) \approx \frac{s(t+h) - s(t)}{h}
$$

 

at the time $t=0.1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=0.1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{′}(0.1) & ≈\frac{s(0.1+0.1)-s(0.1)}{0.1} \\  & =\frac{s(0.2)-s(0.1)}{0.1} \\  & =\frac{7-3}{0.1} \\  & =\frac{4}{0.1} \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

So at $t=0.1$ the velocity is approximately $40\, \textrm{ft}/\textrm{s}.$

e-154.problem:
An oil tank has leaked $q(t)$ liters of oil after $t$ hours. The graph of $q(t)$ is shown below. Approximate the rate at which the oil is leaking from the tank when $t=1$ using a forward difference approximation with step size $h=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14057748/assets/b6c5286dae7e739a588173bad9c721ae34d07f86e455e44ec9f229628cf54211.png)
e-154.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
q'(t) \approx \frac{q(t+h) - q(t)}{h}
$$

 

at the time $t=1$ with step size $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{q(1+1)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(2)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, after $1$ hour, the tank is leaking oil at a rate of approximately $1\,\textrm{liter}/ \textrm{hour}.$

The graph of the function $y=g(x)$ is shown above. Approximate ${g}^{′}(x)$ at the point $x=1.5$ using a forward difference approximation with step size $h=1.$
content.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{g}^{′}(x)≈\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}{h}
$$

 
at the point $x=1.5.$ Applying the above formula with $x=1.5$ and $h=1$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(1.5) & ≈\frac{g(1.5+1)-g(1.5)}{1} \\  & =\frac{g(2.5)-g(1.5)}{1} \\  & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{s}^{′}(t)≈\frac{s(t+h)-s(t)}{h}
$$

 
at the point $t=6.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{′}(6) & ≈\frac{s(6+2)-s(6)}{2} \\  & =\frac{s(8)-s(6)}{2} \\  & =\frac{20-15}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2} \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So at $t=6$ Andrey's speed is approximately $2.5\,\text{m/s}.$

The power of a mobile phone emitter increases when the phone is switched on. The power output of the emitter after $t$ minutes is given by $W(t),$ where $W$ is measured in watts. The graph of $W(t)$ is shown above. 
Approximate the rate of increase in the power of the emitter when $t=1$ using a forward difference approximation with step size $h=2.$
after.worked_solution:
We use the forward difference approximation

$$
{W}^{′}(t)≈\frac{W(t+h)-W(t)}{h},
$$

 
at the time $t=1$ with step size $h=2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{W(1+2)-W(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{W(3)-W(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{100-50}{2} \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

So, after $1$ minute, the power is increasing at a rate of approximately $25\,\text{watts}/\text{minute}.$
